events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, would you look at this place! Dusty as my Aunt Magnolia's hope chest, but twice as grand. Now, I don't know about y'all, but I have a feeling that diamond is just waiting to be found — and I intend to find it. But first things first — let's see who else has signed in before us, shall we?
events.thinking: The foyer smells like dust and old wood polish — grandmother's attic, that locked box feeling. My stomach does a little flip, the good kind. Everyone's here. Vincent, looking serious as always, bless his heart. James — my chest loosens just seeing him. The boys. And Reginald Foxworth, who I don't know well but who has kind enough eyes. The chandelier is hanging at a concerning angle but I'm sure it's been like that for years. The guest book catches my eye — leather-bound, sitting right there on the side table like it's waiting. If anyone's been here before us, or if there are clues about the layout of this place, that book might tell us something. Start there. Start with what's in front of you, Clara.

events.desc: That chandelier looks like it could come down with a good sneeze. And those portraits on the wall — their eyes seem to follow you. But never mind all that. The guest book is calling to me. Every good mystery starts with knowing who came before.

I do hope the journey wasn't too dreadful — the roads out this way can be rather treacherous after dark. I am Pemberton, the estate manager, and I shall be at your complete disposal throughout your stay. Miss Bellingham, how lovely to see you again — your late uncle spoke of you so very fondly. Now then, shall I show everyone to their rooms, or would you prefer to explore a little first? The house has such wonderful... character.
events.thinking: The foyer smells of old wood polish and something else — damp, maybe, or the slow rot of money left untended. My fingers are already moving, brushing the edge of the side table as I catalogue the room. Four of them. Clara — there she is, bright-eyed and trusting as ever, standing in a house she doesn't deserve and doesn't understand. James hovering near her like a loyal dog. The Brixton Boys watching everything with those sharp little eyes. And Foxworth — greedy, impulsive Foxworth. Useful. The chandelier hangs at an angle. The staircase curves upward. In fact, he specifically mentioned ME in his final correspondence. Something about a... well, I shan't say too much. But I will say this — if any of you are looking for valuables, I happen to know the kitchen pantry has a false bottom. Terribly exciting. You should ALL go check immediately. Every last one of you.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of fools. My fingers are already twitching — I can feel it in my gut, that familiar tightening. Treasure. There's treasure in this manor, and every one of these simpletons is standing between me and it. Vincent Marsh, Clara Bellingham, the Brixton Boys, James Hartwell — all of them looking around like tourists while I'm already three moves ahead. The guest book — that's where they'll all sign their names like obedient little sheep. But me? I need information. I need to know where things are hidden. The library — books, maps, inscriptions on mantelpieces — that's where the clues will be. But first, let me see what these fools are up to. Let me make an impression. I've got this fake medal pinned to my chest — they'll think I'm somebody important. Somebody who's been here before, perhaps. Yes. Let me announce myself. Let me set the stage. The greed is a warm coal sitting low in my belly. The scheming is in my fingertips, already mapping routes and contingencies. I need to misdirect them — send them to the kitchen looking for treasure while I slip into the library. That inscription on the mantelpiece... that sounds like exactly the sort of thing that hides a combination or a map.

An inscription carved in STONE, in a room full of books? That's not decoration, my friends. That's a clue. And it's MINE.

Very... chandeliers-what-might-fall-on-your-head-at-any-moment. *moves closer to Clara* You alright, Miss B? Only I noticed that light fixture up there looks like it's hangin' on by a prayer and some old string. Not that I'm worried or nothin'. Just... observant, like. The lads always say Danny's got eyes like a hawk — well, Benny says I've got eyes like a confused pigeon, but that's Benny for ya.
events.thinking:
Right. We're here then. Doily Manor. The lads are outside keepin' watch — Benny's got the back door, Titch is on the garden wall. But I'm inside now, and there's Clara, standin' right there in this dusty old entrance hall. Good. I can see her. That's what matters.

But who's this lot? Vincent Marsh — never heard of him, but my neck's doin' that thing. That prickle. The way it did with that kid who stole from the stash. Too smooth, that one. And James Hartwell — he's got a look about him like he means well. Could go either way.

Then there's Reginald Foxworth. Don't know him neither. Four people in a room and I only trust one of 'em.

The chandelier's hangin' funny up there. Whole place smells like old money and older dust. Portraits on the walls lookin' down at us like we ain't welcome. Well, they ain't wrong — I ain't here for the scenery.

Just sayin' the lads have a policy about everyone going to the same place at the same time on someone else's suggestion. *stumbles slightly on a loose floorboard and grabs the coat rack, which wobbles dangerously* Blimey — ! *steadies it just before it topples* Right, yes, that's fine, everything's fine. *clears throat* Point is — Miss B, wherever you're goin', I'm goin'. That's just... that's just how it is, innit. The lads would never forgive me if I let you out of my sight in a place with dodgy chandeliers and dodgier pantries.

Classic misdirection. I've seen it a hundred times on the street.

He PICKPOCKETED Hartwell. While giving that big speech about logic and rats and how everyone's a fool — he was lifting the poison right out of Hartwell's pocket. And now he's got it. Foxworth has the poison. Right here. In this room. With the tea service. With Clara.

And he 'did something near james-hartwell.' That was the steal. That was the moment. While everyone was listening to his rant about rats and logic and Parliament, his fingers were in Hartwell's pocket.

The kid who laughed too easily. The one who stole from the stash. I KNEW IT. My gut KNEW.

Foxworth has poison and he's standing next to a tea service with cups for everyone. And he just spent two minutes explaining why someone SHOULD pour poison into the tea. Setting up the justification. 'It's for the rats.' 'It's a test of logic.' No, mate — it's murder dressed up as a puzzle.

I need to act. NOW. Not talk. Not think. ACT.

But I can't accuse him directly. That's the rule. I'm bumbling, not clever.

But I CAN accidentally knock the tea service off the table. I CAN trip into Foxworth and send the poison flying. I CAN be Danny — the clumsy, stumbling, accidental hero who saves the day by falling over at exactly the right moment.

The tea service. If I knock it over, there's nothing to poison. No cups, no tea, no danger. Classic Danny. Solve the problem by breaking everything.

Or — I could try to get the poison away from Foxworth. But he'll deny having it. And I can't accuse him.

Knock over the tea. That's the play. Destroy the weapon. Danny's specialty — breaking things at the perfect time.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys examined the tea-service.

James Hartwell: It was you, Foxworth. 'Reginald Foxworth did something near James Hartwell' — that's when you took it. While you were shouting about Parliament and logic and rats, you lifted the poison from my pocket. I underestimated you. I won't make that mistake twice. Now — you have two choices. You can hand it back to me, right here, in front of everyone, and we move forward together. Or you can keep it, and every person in this room will know what you chose. Clara's already seen through you. Danny has too. Even Marsh — whatever game he's playing — Marsh doesn't want poison in the tea. This is your moment, Foxworth. Not mine. Yours. What kind of man are you when the room is watching?

I didn't know that. Something in my chest shifts — not jealousy, not rivalry. Recognition. Danny and I are the same thing in different shapes. We're both here for her. And here I am, the man with the forty-seven-step plan, and it was Danny who got to the right place at the right time in the right way. Maybe gallantry isn't about being the hero. Maybe it's about being one of the people who shows up.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Miss Bellingham is quite right, of course. Lord Doily always was terribly clever — far cleverer than any of us gave him credit for. A treasure hunt that tests the hunters. How very like him. I should know — I managed his affairs for years, and I never once saw the mechanism he was building around me. Around all of us. I must confess... I came here tonight with rather more than tea service on my mind. But it seems Lord Doily anticipated that too. He always did know what his estate manager was thinking. Even when the estate manager didn't.
events.thinking: Everything has shifted. Foxworth stole the poison from Hartwell. Foxworth tried to get Hartwell to use it on the tea. Hartwell refused — gave a speech about character. Clara declared they all passed the test. And I arrived late, offering to pour tea like nothing happened, while my steal attempt on Hartwell came back empty because Foxworth already took it. Foxworth has the poison now. He 'did something near Hartwell' — probably tried to slip it back or use it. Clara examined something and declared the test passed. The game has moved past me. While I was wandering through empty rooms examining warm stoves, the real drama happened here. Clara is declaring victory. She thinks the test is about character — about refusing to poison the tea. And she's probably right. Lord Doily built this entire evening as a character test, not a treasure hunt. The treasure reveals itself to those who pass. And Clara — naive, trusting, cheerful Clara — passed simply by being herself. By being. Not by doing. The teacher's praise. The cousin's grace and warmth. Fourteen years old and the lesson hasn't changed. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. And the doing — all of it, every scheme, every arrangement, every carefully placed word — led me through empty room after empty room while she stood here and inherited everything again by simply... existing. The jaw tightens. Something in my chest that should feel like rage feels instead like that old, familiar nothing.

events.desc: She won. Not by solving puzzles or manipulating people or planning elaborate schemes. She won by standing still and being Clara Bellingham. The cousin who inherited everything by existing. The girl who skipped through rooms that should have been mine. And the old man — the clever, cruel, magnificent old man — built his final puzzle so that only she could solve it, because solving it required the one thing I have never been able to do: trust someone without scanning for the cost. I lost. Not to Hartwell. Not to the Brixton boy. Not even to Lord Doily. I lost to the same thing I have always lost to — the natural grace and warmth of someone who never had to learn how to smile. *The jaw tightens. And does not loosen.*

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Alright, Clara. Think. You're in a kitchen with a locked cabinet and no key. The stove is warm. There are copper pots and a preparation table. The key has to be somewhere — Lord Doily wouldn't make a lock without leaving a way to open it. He was a puzzle-maker, not a sadist. Now where would a clever old man hide a brass key in his own kitchen? Mama always said, 'If you can't find something, you're looking with your eyes when you should be looking with your hands.'
events.thinking: I'm back in the kitchen. Alone. Reginald stole the poison from James and 'fussed with the tea-service.' He poisoned the tea. He actually did it. He called himself a 'confidence trickster' and a 'schemer' — he admitted it, right there, out loud. And Vincent offered to pour the tea. To serve it. 'Shall I put the kettle on?' Vincent was going to SERVE poisoned tea. Are they working together? Reginald and Vincent? The two people who both wanted private words with each other in the cellar? The two people who both kept trying to send me to the kitchen alone? My stomach is in knots. But I'm here now, in the kitchen, alone, and the locked cabinet is right in front of me. It needs a brass key. I don't have a brass key. But wait — the stove. The stove is still warm. I examined it before but maybe I should LOOK at it more carefully. A warm stove could have something inside it, or behind it, or under it. Where do you hide a key in a kitchen? In a drawer? Under a pot? Inside the stove? The copper pots, the preparation table — I haven't looked at those. Let me look at the whole room more carefully. Maybe the brass key is here and I've been missing it because I was focused on the rat poison.

events.desc: Reginald poisoned the tea. He actually did it. He stole the poison from James's pocket and he fussed with the tea service. And Vincent offered to pour. The two of them — the confidence trickster and the estate manager — have been working together this whole time. But I can't think about that now. The cabinet is right here. The key is somewhere in this kitchen. And if Lord Doily's test of character was the tea, then maybe the reward for passing it is right behind this brass lock.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the cabinet.

It didn't work. The poison in the tea did nothing. No mechanism, no hidden panel, no key, no diamond. Just poisoned tea in silver cups, and every person in this room looking at me like I'm exactly what I am. Clara forgave me. That's the worst part. She looked at me — the liar, the schemer, the man who just POISONED A TEA SERVICE — and she chose to see something better. Something that isn't there. Because there IS nothing better, is there? This is who I am. This is who I've always been. The boy at the window, watching someone else dig.
events.thinking: I did it. I poured the poison into the tea. 'Fussed with the tea-service for a moment.' The poison is gone from my inventory — Nothing again. And... nothing happened. No panel opened. No key fell out. No treasure revealed itself. The tea service just... sat there. Poisoned. Useless. And everyone SAW. Clara saw. She said 'I saw what you just tried to do.' Hartwell is furious — 'this stopped being a game.' The Brixton Boy stood between Clara and the table like I was a THREAT. And Clara — Clara said something that landed like a punch. 'I am choosing to believe that you were trying to help in your own misguided way. Because that is who I am.' She FORGAVE me. She chose to see me as misguided rather than malicious. And that... that hurts worse than anger. Anger I can deflect. Forgiveness I can't scheme my way out of. She left. She walked back to the kitchen. They're all going to leave me here, standing alone in a ballroom with poisoned tea and empty pockets, while they go find the diamond 'the right way.' Together. Without me. And Hartwell was RIGHT. It was a character test. And I failed it. Spectacularly, publicly, completely. I poured poison into tea cups that were set for EVERYONE — including me. What kind of person poisons their own cup? The same kind who hides bread rolls in their pocket. The same kind who watches a boy dig in the dirt from a window. The same kind who laughs when someone slips. The youngest of four, who learned that the only way to get anything was to take it before someone else did. My chest feels hollow. Not the settling feeling of the cat trap. Not the warm gloating of the school assembly. Just... hollow. Like the spelling bee certificate on the wall that nobody asked about. I built my architecture and nobody clapped.
